How Fast Should a Model Commit to Supervision?
Training Reasoning Models on the Tsallis Loss Continuum

Chu-Cheng Lin    Eugene Ie Affiliation: Google Email: {kitsing,eugeneie}@google.com
Abstract

Adapting reasoning models to new tasks during post-training with only output-level supervision stalls under reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) when the initial success probability p0p_{0} is small. Using the Tsallis qq-logarithm, we define a loss family JQJ_{Q} that interpolates between RLVR (at q=0q{=}0, the exploitation pole) and the log-marginal-likelihood over latent trajectories (at q=1q{=}1, the density-estimation pole). All members share the same per-example gradient direction, differing only by a scalar amplification P𝜽−qP_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{-q} that reweights each instance independently of the learning rate. This amplification is the mechanism that addresses cold-start stalling: under gradient flow, the exploitation pole requires Ω⁡(1/p0)\Omega(\nicefrac{{1}}{{p_{0}}}) time to escape cold start, while the density-estimation pole escapes in Θ⁡(log⁡(1/p0))\Theta\big(\log(\nicefrac{{1}}{{p_{0}}})\big); intermediate qq trades escape speed against noise memorization. Because P𝜽P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}} is intractable, we derive two Monte Carlo estimators from the two factorizations of the gradient: Gradient-Amplified RL (GARL) samples from the prior and amplifies the RL gradient, and Posterior-Attenuated Fine-Tuning (PAFT) importance-resamples from the posterior and runs standard SFT. Both have bias O⁡(q/M​P𝜽q+1)O\big(\nicefrac{{q}}{{MP_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{q+1}}}\big); GARL has lower variance, PAFT has semantically coherent gradients. On FinQA, HotPotQA, and MuSiQue, GARL at q=0.75q{=}0.75 substantially mitigates cold-start stalling, escaping cold start where GRPO fails entirely. In warm start, GARL at low qq dominates FinQA where training is stable; on HotPotQA and MuSiQue, GARL destabilizes during training, and PAFT at q=0.75q{=}0.75 provides stable gradients (best overall on HotPotQA at 47.9 maj@16, +14.4+14.4 over GRPO).

1 Introduction

Language models reason most effectively when they generate latent computational trajectories  — chains of thought, proof sketches, search traces  — before producing an answer (Lin et al., 2021; Merrill and Sabharwal, 2024). Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) (DeepSeek-AI, 2025; Shao et al., 2024) is commonly used to learn such reasoning models, where the latent rationales are action sequences for reaching correct answers. With supervision only at the output level, RLVR can be prohibitively slow at cold start, when the initial model is too unaligned to make progress. Rao–Blackwellized rewards (Zhou et al., 2026) ensure non-zero reward (and thus non-zero gradients) for all trajectories, but as we show, this reduces gradient variance without addressing the escape-speed bottleneck. Even when RLVR succeeds, it is mode-seeking, and the reasoning capability boundary can narrow as training proceeds (Yue et al., 2025), limiting sample diversity and self-consistency decoding (Wang et al., 2023). Instruction engineering supplies enough structure for SFT and RL to progress (Ouyang et al., 2022; DeepSeek-AI, 2025; Chu et al., 2025), but the recipe depends on task-specific prompts, and naive SFT on weak annotations risks memorizing label errors (Zhang and Sabuncu, 2018). The two failure modes  — cold-start stagnation and noise memorization  — pull in opposite directions, and a unifying theoretical account has been lacking.

We provide such an account, built around a per-instance gradient amplification that directly addresses the cold-start stalling problem. Let P𝜽=p𝜽​(𝐲∗∣𝐱∗)P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}=p_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}({{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*}) denote the model’s conditional success probability. We show that exploitation and density estimation behaviors arise as two endpoints (or poles) of a one-parameter loss continuum JQJ_{Q} derived from this quantity, under the Tsallis qq-logarithm (Tsallis, 1988): the exploitation pole J0=𝔼[1−P𝜽]J_{0}=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[1-P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}] (maximization of expected accuracy, equivalent to RLVR under exact-match reward11 1 Following Zhou et al. (2026), our framework assumes exact-match supervision R⁡(𝐲^,𝐲∗)=𝕀⁡(𝐲^=𝐲∗)R(\hat{{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*})=\mathbb{I}(\hat{{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}}={{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}), which enables the Rao–Blackwellized reward wm=p𝜽​(𝐲∗∣𝐱∗,𝐳)w_{m}=p_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}({{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}). Gold input-output pairs are readily available in supervised settings, while task-specific reward functions are not. Extending to general rewards is an interesting direction but beyond our scope.) and the density-estimation pole J1=𝔼[−log⁡P𝜽]J_{1}=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[-\log P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}] (maximization of log\log-marginal-likelihood over latent trajectories). All members share the same per-example gradient direction, differing only by a scalar amplification P𝜽−qP_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{-q} (Figure 1): qq, which we denote as commitment, amplifies the pull on low-P𝜽P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}} (unfamiliar) examples relative to high-P𝜽P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}} (familiar) ones. Since the learning rate sets one global step size for all examples, no global learning rate can exactly reproduce this per-instance reweighting. This amplification is precisely what is absent from RLVR’s success-probability dynamics, and is the mechanism that addresses cold-start stalling.

Commitment is thus the training-time analog of the inference-time exploration-exploitation tradeoff studied in RL (Lee et al., 2018; Nachum et al., 2018): low qq concentrates on what the model already knows, high qq pushes toward unfamiliar supervision. High commitment (q→1q\to 1) resolves ambiguity  — escaping cold start in Θ⁡(log⁡(1/p0))\Theta(\log(\nicefrac{{1}}{{p_{0}}})) time (Theorem 5.2)  — but memorizes noise, since the model fits the training distribution exactly, including errors (Zhang and Sabuncu, 2018). Low commitment (q→0q\to 0) resolves noise  — the bounded loss and escort tempering filter corrupted labels (Proposition C.2)  — but escape slows to Ω⁡(1/p0)\Omega(\nicefrac{{1}}{{p_{0}}}) (Theorem 5.1). Intermediate qq balances this tradeoff between ambiguity resolution and noise resistance.

Because P𝜽P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}} is intractable, practical optimization requires Monte Carlo estimation. The gradient admits two factorizations  — through the RL and FT endpoints (Figure 2)  — each of which extends a classical estimator at its endpoint to the full continuum. The two resulting methods are complementary: one uses all MM sampled rationales but mixes in contributions that may contradict the answer; the other approximately samples from the posterior over rationales that agree with the answer and runs standard fine-tuning on them, trading statistical efficiency for semantically coherent gradients. Both have the same bias; the choice is dictated by the training regime.

Overview of contributions.

Figures 1 and 2 visualize the loss continuum and the gradient duality; our contributions follow from the P𝜽−qP_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}^{-q} amplification factor (Proposition 4.1).

  1. 1.

    The JQJ_{Q} loss family (Sections 3, 4 and 5). JQJ_{Q} interpolates between a bounded, noise-robust loss at q=0q=0 and an unbounded, mode-covering loss at q=1q=1, with minimizers given by the escort distribution θj∗∝αj1/q\theta_{j}^{*}\propto\alpha_{j}^{1/q} (Theorem 3.1)  — a training-time analog of inference temperature  — and a dispersion penalty that encourages uniform success across training examples (Proposition B.1). All members share the same gradient direction, differing only by P𝜽−qP_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{-q}, which controls cold-start escape speed: the exploitation pole cannot escape faster than Ω⁡(1/p0)\Omega(\nicefrac{{1}}{{p_{0}}}) (Theorem 5.1), while the density-estimation pole escapes in Θ⁡(log⁡(1/p0))\Theta(\log(1/p_{0})) (Theorem 5.2).

  2. 2.

    Two gradient estimators: GARL and PAFT (Section 6). The gradient admits two factorizations  — via the RL endpoint (P𝜽−q​∇𝜽ℓ0P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{-q}\,\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}\ell_{0}) and the FT endpoint (P𝜽1−q​∇𝜽ℓ1P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{1-q}\,\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}\ell_{1})  — each yielding a practical Monte Carlo estimator. Gradient-Amplified RL (GARL) samples trajectories from the prior and amplifies the RL gradient, generalizing RB-REINFORCE (Zhou et al., 2026, q=0q{=}0;) and the IWAE gradient estimator (Burda et al., 2015, q=1q{=}1;). Posterior-Attenuated Fine-Tuning (PAFT) approximately samples from the posterior p𝜽​(𝐳∣𝐱∗,𝐲∗)p_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}({{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}) over rationales that agree with the answer and runs standard fine-tuning on them, generalizing the E-step of EM (Dempster et al., 1977; Phan et al., 2023, q=1q{=}1;). Both have the same bias O⁡(q/M​P𝜽q+1)O(\nicefrac{{q}}{{MP_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{q+1}}}); GARL has lower variance, PAFT produces semantically coherent gradients. GARL is essential at cold start (posterior sampling yields no trajectories); in warm start, GARL at low qq works when training is stable (FinQA), but destabilizes on HotPotQA and MuSiQue. PAFT does not collapse on any benchmark we tested, at the cost of slower per-step learning (Section 7).

  3. 3.

    Empirical validation (Section 7). On three reasoning benchmarks (FinQA, HotPotQA, MuSiQue) with strict (exact-match) training rewards, GARL at intermediate qq escapes cold start where GRPO fails entirely. At warm start, the best stable method at each benchmark improves maj@16 over GRPO by +6.6+6.6 to +14.4+14.4 points: GARL at q=0.25q{=}0.25 leads on FinQA (38.738.7 vs. 26.926.9) where training is stable; PAFT at q=0.75q{=}0.75 is best on HotPotQA (47.947.9 vs. 33.533.5) where GARL collapses at all tested qq, and on MuSiQue (22.422.4 vs. 15.815.8) where GARL’s higher peak does not survive training.

2 Setup and Background

We consider supervised conditional generation with latent reasoning trajectories. Let 𝚯⊆ℝd{\bm{\mathbf{\Theta}}}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} be the parameter space of an autoregressive language model p𝜽p_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}} with alphabet Σ\Sigma. Inputs come from a task distribution we do not model. We train on a supervised dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} of input-output pairs (𝐱∗,𝐲∗)({{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}), where 𝐱∗∈𝒳⊆Σ∗{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*}\in\mathcal{X}\subseteq\Sigma^{*} and 𝐲∗∈𝒴⊆Σ∗{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}\in\mathcal{Y}\subseteq\Sigma^{*}.

Generative story.

Given input 𝐱{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}, the model samples an unannotated latent rationale 𝐳∈𝒵⊆Σ∗{{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}\in\mathcal{Z}\subseteq\Sigma^{*} from p𝜽(⋅∣𝐱)p_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}(\cdot\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}), then generates an output 𝐲^∼p𝜽(⋅∣𝐱,𝐳)\hat{{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}}\sim p_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}(\cdot\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}},{{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}). This defines the joint p𝜽​(𝐳,𝐲∣𝐱)=p𝜽​(𝐳∣𝐱)​p𝜽​(𝐲∣𝐱,𝐳)p_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}({{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}})=p_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}({{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}})\,p_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}({{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}},{{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}) and the induced marginal p𝜽​(𝐲∣𝐱)=∑𝐳∈𝒵p𝜽​(𝐳,𝐲∣𝐱)p_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}({{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}})=\sum_{{{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}\in\mathcal{Z}}p_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}({{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}).22 2 Since 𝒵⊆Σ∗\mathcal{Z}\subseteq\Sigma^{*} is at most countable, we write finite sums over 𝒵\mathcal{Z}; results extend to countably infinite 𝒵\mathcal{Z} under dominated convergence.

The latent 𝐳{{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}} may represent a chain of thought (Wei et al., 2022), proof trace, search trajectory, program, or other internal computational object. We treat 𝐳{{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}} as an operational latent: with supervision only at the output level, the latent trajectory mediates the output distribution.

Success probability and endpoint losses.

For each supervised example (𝐱∗,𝐲∗)({{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}), the central quantity is the success probability P𝜽≜p𝜽​(𝐲∗∣𝐱∗)P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}\triangleq p_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}({{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*}). From this we define two endpoint losses: the exploitation loss J0​(𝜽)≜𝔼(𝐱∗,𝐲∗)∼𝒟[1−P𝜽]J_{0}({\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}})\triangleq\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{{({{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*})\sim\mathcal{D}}}[1-P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}] and the density-estimation loss J1​(𝜽)≜𝔼(𝐱∗,𝐲∗)∼𝒟[−log⁡P𝜽]J_{1}({\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}})\triangleq\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{{({{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*})\sim\mathcal{D}}}[-\log P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}]. Both are minimized at 00 when P𝜽=1P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}=1, but transform P𝜽P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}} into optimization signal differently. Under exact-match supervision (R⁡(𝐲^,𝐲∗)=𝕀⁡(𝐲^=𝐲∗)R(\hat{{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*})=\mathbb{I}(\hat{{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}}={{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*})), J0J_{0} equals 11 minus the expected reward (Proposition A.1), so minimizing J0J_{0} is equivalent to maximizing expected reward.33 3 Full proofs of all proof sketches are in the appendix, organized by section.

The JQJ_{Q} family.

We interpolate using the Tsallis qq-logarithm (Tsallis, 1988):

logq⁡(u)=u1−q−11−q,0<u≤1,\displaystyle\log_{q}(u)=\frac{u^{1-q}-1}{1-q},\quad 0<u\leq 1, (1)

with log1⁡(u)≜limq→1logq⁡(u)=log⁡u\log_{1}(u)\triangleq\lim_{q\to 1}\log_{q}(u)=\log u. We define the loss family

JQ​(𝜽,q)\displaystyle J_{Q}({\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}},q) =𝔼(𝐱∗,𝐲∗)∼𝒟[−logq⁡(P𝜽)],\displaystyle=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{{({{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*})\sim\mathcal{D}}}[-\log_{q}(P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}})], (2)

or equivalently

JQ​(𝜽,q)\displaystyle J_{Q}({\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}},q) =𝔼(𝐱∗,𝐲∗)∼𝒟[−logq⁡(∑𝐳∈𝒵p𝜽​(𝐳,𝐲∗∣𝐱∗))].\displaystyle=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{{({{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*})\sim\mathcal{D}}}[-\log_{q}\Big(\sum_{{{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}\in\mathcal{Z}}p_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}({{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*})\Big)].

It recovers the endpoints: JQ​(𝜽,0)=J0​(𝜽)J_{Q}({\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}},0)=J_{0}({\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}) and JQ​(𝜽,1)=J1​(𝜽)J_{Q}({\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}},1)=J_{1}({\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}).

3 Loss Landscape of the JQJ_{Q} Continuum

For a fixed supervised example (𝐱∗,𝐲∗)({{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}), define the per-example qq-loss

ℓq​(𝜽,𝐱∗,𝐲∗)≜−logq⁡P𝜽=1−P𝜽1−q1−q,\displaystyle\ell_{q}({\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}};{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*})\triangleq-\log_{q}P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}=\frac{1-P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}^{1-q}}{1-q}, (3)

so that JQ​(𝜽,q)=𝔼(𝐱∗,𝐲∗)∼𝒟[ℓq​(𝜽,𝐱∗,𝐲∗)]J_{Q}({\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}},q)=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{{({{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*})\sim\mathcal{D}}}[\ell_{q}({\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}};{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*})]. At q=0q=0 this gives ℓ0=1−P𝜽\ell_{0}=1-P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}} (bounded in [0,1][0,1]); at q=1q=1 it gives ℓ1=−log⁡P𝜽\ell_{1}=-\log P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}} (unbounded as P𝜽→0P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}\to 0). The parameter qq shapes the loss landscape in four ways:

  • •

    Dataset-level coverage: q>0q>0 penalizes non-uniform success across training examples (dispersion penalty).

  • •

    Prediction-level coverage: the minimizer is the escort distribution θj∗∝αj1/q\theta_{j}^{*}\propto\alpha_{j}^{1/q}, interpolating from mode-seeking (q→0q\to 0) to mode-covering (q=1q=1).

  • •

    Propriety: q=1q=1 is the unique strictly proper scoring rule in the family; q<1q<1 introduces controlled mode-seeking bias.

  • •

    Robustness: at q<1q<1 the loss is bounded and the escort tempering concentrates the minimizer away from corrupted labels; at q=1q=1 the model fits noise exactly.

We develop the first two below; formal statements for all four are in Appendix B.

3.1 Dataset-level coverage: the dispersion penalty

Let P¯≜𝔼(𝐱∗,𝐲∗)∼𝒟[P𝜽]\bar{P}\triangleq\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{{({{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*})\sim\mathcal{D}}}[P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}] denote the mean success probability. The exploitation loss J0=1−P¯J_{0}=1-\bar{P} depends only on P¯\bar{P} and is indifferent to how success is distributed across examples. For q>0q>0, −logq-\log_{q} is strictly convex, so Jensen’s inequality gives JQ≥−logq⁡(P¯)J_{Q}\geq-\log_{q}(\bar{P}): the loss penalizes non-uniform success. To second order, the excess loss scales as q2​P¯−q−1​𝐕𝐚𝐫𝒟​(P𝜽)\frac{q}{2}\bar{P}^{-q-1}\,\mathbf{Var}_{\mathcal{D}}(P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}), with the penalty coefficient monotonically increasing in qq.

3.2 Prediction-level coverage: the escort minimizer

At the prediction level, qq controls whether the model’s output distribution matches the data or concentrates on the mode. Consider a categorical model with a single input 𝐱∗{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*}, outputs {v1,…,vN}\{v_{1},\dots,v_{N}\}, model p𝜽​(vj∣𝐱∗)=θj∈ΔNp_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}(v_{j}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*})=\theta_{j}\in\Delta_{N}, and empirical frequencies αj>0\alpha_{j}>0 with ∑jαj=1\sum_{j}\alpha_{j}=1.

The escort distribution (Beck and Schögl, 1993) of order β\beta of a distribution α\alpha is αjβ/∑kαkβ\nicefrac{{\alpha_{j}^{\beta}}}{{\sum_{k}\alpha_{k}^{\beta}}}; setting β=1/q\beta=\nicefrac{{1}}{{q}} gives the data distribution tempered at temperature qq.

3.1.

[Minimizers of JQJ_{Q} in the categorical model] For q∈(0,1]q\in(0,1], the unique minimizer of JQ​(𝛉,q)=∑jαj​(−logq⁡θj)J_{Q}({\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}},q)=\sum_{j}\alpha_{j}(-\log_{q}\theta_{j}) over ΔN\Delta_{N} is the escort distribution of order 1/q\nicefrac{{1}}{{q}}:

θj∗(q)=αj1/q∑k=1Nαk1/q,j=1,…,N.\displaystyle\theta_{j}^{*}(q)=\frac{\alpha_{j}^{1/q}}{\sum_{k=1}^{N}\alpha_{k}^{1/q}},\qquad j=1,\dots,N. (4)

For q=0q=0, the objective is linear and minimized at any vertex eje_{j} with j∈argmaxkαkj\in\argmax_{k}\alpha_{k}.

Proof sketch.

For q>0q>0, strict convexity ensures uniqueness. Lagrange multipliers give αj​θj−q=μ\alpha_{j}\theta_{j}^{-q}=\mu for all jj, yielding θj∝αj1/q\theta_{j}\propto\alpha_{j}^{1/q}. ∎

The escort distribution interpolates continuously from full coverage (q=1q=1: θ∗=α\theta^{*}=\alpha) to pure mode seeking (q→0q\to 0: θ∗\theta^{*} concentrates on the most frequent output). In particular, q=1q=1 is the unique strictly proper scoring rule in the JQJ_{Q} family (Corollary B.3).

4 Gradient Geometry of JQJ_{Q}

All members of JQJ_{Q} share the same per-example gradient direction. The gradient factors through either the RL endpoint ∇𝜽ℓ0\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}\ell_{0} or the FT endpoint ∇𝜽ℓ1\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}\ell_{1}, motivating the two Monte Carlo estimators of Section 6.

4.1Gradient geometry and dual factorization.

For any fixed supervised example (𝐱∗,𝐲∗)({{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}) with P𝛉>0P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}>0 and any q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1],

∇𝜽ℓq​(𝜽,𝐱∗,𝐲∗)=P𝜽−q⏟amplify​∇𝜽ℓ0​(𝜽,𝐱∗,𝐲∗)=P𝜽1−q⏟attenuate​∇𝜽ℓ1​(𝜽,𝐱∗,𝐲∗).\displaystyle\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}\ell_{q}({\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}};{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*})\;=\;\underbrace{P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}^{-q}}_{\text{amplify}}\,\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}\ell_{0}({\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}};{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*})\;=\;\underbrace{P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}^{1-q}}_{\text{attenuate}}\,\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}\ell_{1}({\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}};{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}). (5)
Proof.

By the chain rule and dd​u​logq⁡(u)=u−q\frac{d}{du}\log_{q}(u)=u^{-q}: ∇𝜽ℓq=−P𝜽−q​∇𝜽P𝜽=P𝜽−q​∇𝜽ℓ0\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}\ell_{q}=-P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}^{-q}\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}=P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}^{-q}\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}\ell_{0}. Since ∇𝜽ℓ0=−∇𝜽P𝜽=P𝜽​∇𝜽ℓ1\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}\ell_{0}=-\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}=P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}\,\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}\ell_{1}, the second equality follows. ∎

The scalar rescales either the RL endpoint gradient (by P𝜽−q∈[1,∞)P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}^{-q}\in[1,\infty), amplification) or the FT endpoint gradient (by P𝜽1−q∈[0,1]P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}^{1-q}\in[0,1], attenuation). Setting q=0q=0 recovers ∇ℓ0\nabla\ell_{0} (no amplification); q=1q=1 recovers ∇ℓ1\nabla\ell_{1} (no attenuation).

The scalar P𝜽−qP_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}^{-q} controls both cold-start escape speed (p˙=p2−q​‖s‖2\dot{p}=p^{2-q}\|s\|^{2}, yielding the Ω⁡(1/p0)\Omega(\nicefrac{{1}}{{p_{0}}}) versus Θ⁡(log⁡(1/p0))\Theta(\log(1/p_{0})) separation of Section 5) and finite-sample estimator bias (larger qq increases the O⁡(q/(M​P𝜽q+1))O(q/(MP_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{q+1})) bias of Section 6). Each factorization motivates a Monte Carlo estimator: the RL factorization yields GARL (prior sampling with amplification; Section 6.1), the FT factorization yields PAFT (posterior sampling with attenuation; Section 6.2).

5 Commitment Dynamics under Gradient Flow

Under gradient flow, escape from a cold start (p0=P𝜽⁡(0)≪1p_{0}=P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}(0)}\ll 1) takes Ω⁡(1/p0)\Omega(\nicefrac{{1}}{{p_{0}}}) time at the exploitation pole (q=0q{=}0) but only Θ⁡(log⁡(1/p0))\Theta(\log(\nicefrac{{1}}{{p_{0}}})) at the density-estimation pole (q=1q{=}1). This exponential separation in 1/p01/p_{0} is governed by the amplification factor P𝜽−qP_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{-q} and the dynamics p˙=p2−q​‖s⁡(𝜽)‖2\dot{p}=p^{2-q}\|s({\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}})\|^{2}. Our analysis is stylized: it tracks single-example success probability under continuous-time gradient flow, isolating the role of the amplification factor rather than fully modeling multi-example LM optimization.

5.1 Dynamics of the success probability

We study gradient flow, the continuous-time limit of gradient descent, in which parameters evolve as 𝜽˙=−∇𝜽ℓ​(𝜽)\dot{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}=-\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}\ell({\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}) (Su et al., 2016). This removes step-size effects and yields closed-form rates that capture the qualitative behavior of discrete optimization. The results below require no convexity: p˙≥0\dot{p}\geq 0 always (Equation 6), so pp is monotone along the flow.

Fix a single example’s qq-loss ℓq​(𝜽)=−logq⁡(P𝜽)\ell_{q}({\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}})=-\log_{q}(P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}), 𝜽∈ℝd{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. Let p⁡(t)≜P𝜽⁡(t)p(t)\triangleq P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}(t)} denote the success probability along the flow, with time derivative p˙≜d​p/d​t\dot{p}\triangleq\nicefrac{{dp}}{{dt}}. We combine p˙​(t)=∇𝜽P𝜽⁡(t)⋅𝜽˙​(t)\dot{p}(t)=\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}(t)}\cdot\dot{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}(t) (chain rule), and 𝜽˙​(t)=−∇𝜽ℓq​(𝜽⁡(t))=P𝜽⁡(t)−q​∇𝜽P𝜽⁡(t)\dot{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}(t)=-\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}\ell_{q}({\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}(t))=P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}(t)}^{-q}\,\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}(t)} (the second equality uses Proposition 4.1, which gives ∇𝜽ℓq=−P𝜽−q​∇𝜽P𝜽\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}\ell_{q}=-P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{-q}\,\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}). Substituting and writing ∇𝜽P𝜽⁡(t)=P𝜽⁡(t)​∇𝜽​log⁡P𝜽⁡(t)\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}(t)}=P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}(t)}\,\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}\log P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}(t)} with score s⁡(𝜽)≜∇𝜽​log​P𝜽s({\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}})\triangleq\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}\log P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}},

p˙=∇𝜽P𝜽⁡(t)⋅𝜽˙​(t)=∇𝜽P𝜽⁡(t)⋅(P𝜽⁡(t)−q​∇𝜽P𝜽⁡(t))=P𝜽⁡(t)−q​‖∇𝜽P𝜽⁡(t)‖2=p2−q​‖s⁡(𝜽⁡(t))‖2.\displaystyle\dot{p}=\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}(t)}\cdot\dot{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}(t)=\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}(t)}\cdot\big(P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}(t)}^{-q}\,\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}(t)}\big)=P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}(t)}^{-q}\,\|\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}(t)}\|^{2}=p^{2-q}\,\|s({\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}(t))\|^{2}. (6)

The entire effect of qq on convergence speed is captured by the exponent 2−q2-q on pp; the factor ‖s⁡(𝜽)‖2\|s({\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}})\|^{2} depends on the architecture but not on qq.

5.2 Cold-start escape rates

Let p0≜p⁡(0)≪1p_{0}\triangleq p(0)\ll 1. With ‖s‖\|s\| approximately constant, Equation 6 implies that the escape time to a target δ\delta is T∼∫p0δu−(2−q)​𝑑uT\sim\int_{p_{0}}^{\delta}u^{-(2-q)}\,du, and the exponent 2−q2-q controls its growth as p0→0p_{0}\to 0: at q=0q=0 the integrand is u−2u^{-2} and TT diverges as 1/p0\nicefrac{{1}}{{p_{0}}}; at q=1q=1 the integrand is u−1u^{-1} and TT diverges only as log⁡(1/p0)\log(\nicefrac{{1}}{{p_{0}}}) (equivalently, p⁡(t)=p0​etp(t)=p_{0}e^{t} under p˙=p\dot{p}=p). We formalize this separation in two results.44 4 The p2−qp^{2-q} factor in Equation 6 is assumption-free; converting it to escape times needs bounds on ‖s‖\|s\|: an upper bound for Ω⁡(⋅)\Omega(\cdot) on time (Theorem 5.1), and additionally a lower bound for matching Θ⁡(⋅)\Theta(\cdot) rates (Theorem 5.2). The first requires only an upper bound on the score norm and establishes that the exploitation pole is provably slow. The second adds a lower bound and shows the density-estimation pole is provably fast, giving tight Θ⁡(⋅)\Theta(\cdot) rates across the continuum.

5.1.

[Exploitation is provably slow] Let 𝛉∈ℝd{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} parameterize any differentiable model. Consider gradient flow on ℓq​(𝛉)=−logq⁡(P𝛉)\ell_{q}({\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}})=-\log_{q}(P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}), starting from p0=P𝛉⁡(0)∈(0,1/2]p_{0}=P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}(0)}\in(0,1/2] with fixed target δ∈(0,1/2]\delta\in(0,1/2]. Suppose only that ‖s⁡(𝛉⁡(t))‖≤C\|s({\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}(t))\|\leq C throughout the trajectory. Then as p0→0p_{0}\to 0:

Tq​(p0,δ)\displaystyle T_{q}(p_{0},\delta) =Ω⁡(p0−(1−q)1−q)​for ​q∈[0,1),\displaystyle=\Omega\!\left(\frac{p_{0}^{-(1-q)}}{1-q}\right)\;\text{for }q\in[0,1),
T1​(p0,δ)\displaystyle T_{1}(p_{0},\delta) =Ω⁡(log⁡1p0).\displaystyle=\Omega\!\left(\log\frac{1}{p_{0}}\right).

In particular, the exploitation pole cannot escape cold start faster than Ω⁡(1/p0)\Omega(\nicefrac{{1}}{{p_{0}}}).

Proof sketch.

From p˙=p2−q​‖s‖2≤C2​p2−q\dot{p}=p^{2-q}\|s\|^{2}\leq C^{2}p^{2-q}, the success probability grows no faster than C2​p2−qC^{2}p^{2-q}. Integrating: Tq≥1C2​∫p0δu−(2−q)​𝑑uT_{q}\geq\frac{1}{C^{2}}\int_{p_{0}}^{\delta}u^{-(2-q)}\,du, which evaluates to Ω⁡(p0−(1−q)/(1−q))\Omega(\nicefrac{{p_{0}^{-(1-q)}}}{{(1-q)}}). ∎

The upper bound ‖s‖≤C\|s\|\leq C holds for any autoregressive softmax model with bounded parameter-to-logit Jacobian: the per-trajectory score ∇𝜽​log​p​(𝐳,𝐲∗∣𝐱∗)=∑t(eyt−pt)⊤​∇𝜽zt\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}\log p({{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*})=\sum_{t}(e_{y_{t}}-p_{t})^{\top}\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}z_{t} combines bounded softmax residuals with the Jacobian ∇𝜽zt\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}z_{t}, and ss is a posterior expectation of these, so ‖s‖\|s\| is bounded whenever the weights are bounded and activations Lipschitz. No matter how favorable the architecture, the exploitation pole requires escape time at least linear in 1/p01/p_{0}  — a prediction Section 7 confirms: q=0q=0 fails to escape cold start in practice.

5.2.

[Tight cold-start escape rates] Under the same setup as Theorem 5.1, suppose additionally that ‖s⁡(𝛉⁡(t))‖≥c>0\|s({\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}(t))\|\geq c>0 throughout the trajectory. Then:

  1. 1.

    General q∈[0,1)q\in[0,1):

    Tq​(p0,δ)=Θ⁡(p0−(1−q)1−q)​as ​p0→0.\displaystyle T_{q}(p_{0},\delta)=\Theta\!\left(\frac{p_{0}^{-(1-q)}}{1-q}\right)\;\text{as }p_{0}\!\to\!0.
  2. 2.

    Density-estimation pole (q=1q=1):

    T1​(p0,δ)=Θ⁡(log⁡1p0)as ​p0→0.\displaystyle T_{1}(p_{0},\delta)=\Theta\!\left(\log\frac{1}{p_{0}}\right)\quad\text{as }p_{0}\to 0.
  3. 3.

    Speedup ratio: for any q<q′q<q^{\prime} with q′≤1q^{\prime}\leq 1,

    Tq​(p0,δ)Tq′​(p0,δ)→∞as ​p0→0.\displaystyle\frac{T_{q}(p_{0},\delta)}{T_{q^{\prime}}(p_{0},\delta)}\to\infty\quad\text{as }p_{0}\to 0.
Proof sketch.

The lower bound on ‖s‖\|s\| gives p˙≥c2​p2−q\dot{p}\geq c^{2}p^{2-q}, yielding the matching upper bound Tq≤1c2​∫p0δu−(2−q)​𝑑uT_{q}\leq\frac{1}{c^{2}}\int_{p_{0}}^{\delta}u^{-(2-q)}\,du. Combined with Theorem 5.1, this gives the Θ⁡(⋅)\Theta(\cdot) bounds. ∎

Robustness of the separation.

The upper bound ‖s‖≤C\|s\|\leq C alone is enough for Theorem 5.1’s Ω⁡(⋅)\Omega(\cdot) time bound; the additional lower bound ‖s‖≥c\|s\|\geq c is used only to promote this to the matching Θ⁡(⋅)\Theta(\cdot) in Theorem 5.2. The qq-dependent separation itself comes from the assumption-free factor p2−qp^{2-q} in Equation 6, so the ordering across poles survives even where ‖s‖≥c\|s\|\geq c fails  — at a critical point, for instance, every qq stalls equally. Section C.1 works out exact escape times for a sigmoid model.

Why momentum-based optimization cannot substitute for qq.

The parameter qq controls per-instance commitment: how much to prioritize hard instances relative to easy ones. This is orthogonal to the global step size set by the learning rate. Momentum-based adaptive optimizers such as Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2014) adjust per-parameter step sizes aggregated across examples, but cannot compensate for per-example reweighting. The scalars P𝜽−qP_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{-q} (for GARL) and P𝜽1−qP_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{1-q} (for PAFT) are thus preserved under both minibatch SGD and Adam, and the cold-start separation persists in practice.

Noise fitting is symmetric.

The same machinery gives a dual result for label noise: for example, in the binary categorical model with symmetric label-flip rate ϵ\epsilon, the time to grow noise contamination p~=1−p𝜽​(c∣𝐱∗)\tilde{p}=1-p_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}(c\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*}) to target level η\eta scales as Tqnoise​(η)=Θ⁡(ηq+1/((q+1)​ϵ))T_{q}^{\mathrm{noise}}(\eta)=\Theta(\eta^{q+1}/((q+1)\epsilon)), with speedup ratio Tq/Tq′=Θ⁡(η−(q′−q))T_{q}/T_{q^{\prime}}=\Theta(\eta^{-(q^{\prime}-q)}) for q<q′q<q^{\prime} (Proposition C.2). The speedup ratio matches the cold-start speedup Θ⁡(p0−(q′−q))\Theta(p_{0}^{-(q^{\prime}-q)}) exactly in form: the same amplification P𝜽−qP_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{-q} accelerates commitment to clean and corrupted supervision alike, with matching exponents in p0p_{0} and η\eta. High commitment thus compresses both timescales  — the time to resolve ambiguity and the time to memorize noise.

SFT-then-RL asymmetry.

The cold-start escape and noise fitting results explain the familiar SFT-then-RL pipeline (Ouyang et al., 2022; DeepSeek-AI, 2025; Chu et al., 2025). SFT on annotated (input, CoT, answer) triples is the q=1q=1 pole with a degenerate proposal (marginalization collapses onto the supervised CoT), so it escapes in Θ⁡(log⁡(1/p0))\Theta(\log(1/p_{0})) via P𝜽−1P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{-1} amplification; RL (q=0q=0) pays the full Θ⁡(1/p0)\Theta(1/p_{0}) cost. Switching to RL after SFT then halts commitment to noisy annotations: q=1q=1 memorizes noise fastest (T1noise=Θ⁡(η2/ϵ)T_{1}^{\mathrm{noise}}=\Theta(\eta^{2}/\epsilon)) while q=0q=0 does not memorize at all (limq→0+Tqnoise​(η)=∞\lim_{q\to 0^{+}}T_{q}^{\mathrm{noise}}(\eta)=\infty for any η>0\eta>0; Proposition C.2). The JQJ_{Q} continuum replaces this hard switch with a smooth interpolation.

6 Gradient Estimators for JQJ_{Q}

The marginal P𝜽=∑𝐳∈𝒵p𝜽​(𝐳,𝐲∗∣𝐱∗)P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}=\sum_{{{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}\in\mathcal{Z}}p_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}({{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*}) in ∇𝜽JQ\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}J_{Q} is intractable, so we estimate the gradient by Monte Carlo. The dual factorization (Proposition 4.1) yields two natural estimators:

  • •

    GARL (Section 6.1): sample from the prior p𝜽​(𝐳∣𝐱∗)p_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}({{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*}), estimate ∇𝜽ℓ0\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}\ell_{0} and P𝜽P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}} from the same samples, amplify by (w¯M)−q(\bar{w}_{M})^{-q}.

  • •

    PAFT (Section 6.2): approximately sample from the posterior p𝜽​(𝐳∣𝐱∗,𝐲∗)p_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}({{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}), estimate ∇𝜽ℓ1\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}\ell_{1} via teacher forcing, attenuate by (w¯M)1−q(\bar{w}_{M})^{1-q}.

Drop-in compute cost.

Both estimators are drop-in replacements for RB-REINFORCE/RLOO at the same rollout budget. GARL replaces the scalar 11 in RB-RLOO with (w¯M)−q(\bar{w}_{M})^{-q}, reusing the MM prior samples and per-token log-probabilities RB-RLOO already computes (Zhou et al., 2026); the only added work is the scalar (w¯M)−q(\bar{w}_{M})^{-q} and the leave-one-out baseline in Equation 12, both O⁡(M)O(M) in compute. PAFT adds one categorical resample over the MM prior weights, followed by teacher forcing on KK resampled trajectories whose tokens have already been generated. Neither requires forward passes beyond what RL training already does. In our experiments (Section 7), GRPO, GARL, and PAFT all use M=32M=32 rollouts per prompt at training time.

6.1 GARL: Gradient-Amplified RL

6.1.1 A plug-in Monte Carlo estimator

Fix a supervised example (𝐱∗,𝐲∗)({{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}) and draw MM i.i.d. latent trajectories 𝐳(1),…,𝐳(M)∼p𝜽(⋅∣𝐱∗){{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}^{(1)},\dots,{{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}^{(M)}\sim p_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}(\cdot\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*}). Define the per-sample likelihood weight and gradient contribution:

wm≜p𝜽​(𝐲∗∣𝐱∗,𝐳(m)),gm≜−wm​∇𝜽​log⁡p𝜽​(𝐳(m),𝐲∗∣𝐱∗),\displaystyle w_{m}\triangleq p_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}({{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}^{(m)}),\qquad g_{m}\triangleq-w_{m}\,\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}\log p_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}({{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}^{(m)},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*}), (7)

with empirical means w¯M≜1M​∑mwm\bar{w}_{M}\triangleq\tfrac{1}{M}\sum_{m}w_{m} and g¯M≜1M​∑mgm\bar{g}_{M}\triangleq\tfrac{1}{M}\sum_{m}g_{m}. By the log-trick,

𝔼[w¯M]=P𝜽,𝔼[g¯M]=−∑𝐳∇𝜽p𝜽(𝐳,𝐲∗∣𝐱∗)=−∇𝜽P𝜽=∇𝜽ℓ0.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\bar{w}_{M}]=P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}},\qquad\mathbb{E}[\bar{g}_{M}]=-\sum_{{{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}}\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}p_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}({{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*})=-\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}=\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}\ell_{0}. (8)

Plugging these into the RL factorization of Proposition 4.1 yields the plug-in estimator

∇𝜽ℓq^​(q,𝜽,𝐱∗,𝐲∗,M)≜g¯M(w¯M)q.\displaystyle\widehat{\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}\ell_{q}}(q,{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}};{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*},M)\triangleq\frac{\bar{g}_{M}}{(\bar{w}_{M})^{q}}. (9)

The dataset-level estimator of ∇𝜽JQ\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}J_{Q} averages Equation 9 over a minibatch: GARL amplifies the RL gradient g¯M\bar{g}_{M} by the plug-in estimate (w¯M)−q(\bar{w}_{M})^{-q} of P𝜽−qP_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{-q}. At the endpoints, GARL recovers RB-REINFORCE (Zhou et al., 2026, q=0q{=}0;) and the IWAE gradient estimator (Burda et al., 2015, q=1q{=}1;); see Section D.2.

Effective reward.

The effective reward wm/(w¯M)q\nicefrac{{w_{m}}}{{(\bar{w}_{M})^{q}}} has a maximum value of MqM^{q}, and varies along with qq; we divide by MqM^{q} to normalize it to [0,1][0,1] (Appendix D). We use the maximum effective reward across samples to monitor training dynamics (Figure 3). The 1/Mq1/M^{q} factor in Algorithms 1 and 2 is an implementation choice equivalent to a qq-dependent learning-rate rescaling; the mathematical estimators of Equations 12 and 14 target ∇𝜽ℓq\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}\ell_{q} directly without it.

6.1.2 Consistency and finite-sample bias

Equation 9 is a ratio estimator: it reuses the same samples in numerator and denominator, so it is biased at finite MM even though w¯M\bar{w}_{M} and g¯M\bar{g}_{M} are individually unbiased.55 5 Assumptions 1–2 of Theorem 6.1 are standard regularity. Assumption 3 holds for autoregressive softmax models: wm=∏t=1Tp𝜽(yt∗∣⋅)w_{m}=\prod_{t=1}^{T}p_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}(y^{*}_{t}\mid\cdot) is a finite product of softmax probabilities bounded below by a logit-dependent ϵ0>0\epsilon_{0}>0, so wm≥ϵ0Tw_{m}\geq\epsilon_{0}^{T}. This is non-vacuous for short outputs but tightens to vanishingly small values for long generations; the bias expansion should accordingly be read as identifying the qualitative direction of finite-sample degradation rather than a uniform numerical bound in the long-sequence regime.

6.1.

[Consistency and bias expansion] Fix a supervised example (𝐱∗,𝐲∗)({{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}) and assume:

  1. 1.

    P𝜽>0P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}>0;

  2. 2.

    𝔼⁡[‖gm‖2]<∞\mathbb{E}[\|g_{m}\|^{2}]<\infty;

  3. 3.

    wm≥ϵw_{m}\geq\epsilon a.s. for some ϵ>0\epsilon>0.

Then for any fixed q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1],

∇𝜽ℓq^​(q,𝜽,𝐱∗,𝐲∗,M)→M→∞a.s.∇𝜽ℓq​(𝜽,q,𝐱∗,𝐲∗).\displaystyle\widehat{\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}\ell_{q}}(q,{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}};{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*},M)\xrightarrow[M\to\infty]{a.s.}\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}\ell_{q}({\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}},q;{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}). (10)

Moreover, for fixed P𝛉>0P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}>0 and q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1], the bias satisfies

𝔼⁡[∇𝜽ℓq^]−∇𝜽ℓq=O⁡(qM​P𝜽q+1)as ​M→∞.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\widehat{\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}\ell_{q}}\right]-\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}\ell_{q}\;=\;O\!\left(\frac{q}{M\,P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}^{q+1}}\right)\quad\text{as }M\to\infty. (11)

At q=0q=0 the factor qq in the numerator makes the bias vanish exactly for all MM: the estimator reduces to the unbiased sample mean g¯M\bar{g}_{M} (Equation 8). The explicit leading-order coefficient is in Appendix D.

Proof sketch.

Assumption 1 ensures continuity of f⁡(a,b)=b​a−qf(a,b)=b\,a^{-q} at (P𝜽,∇ℓ0)(P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}},\nabla\ell_{0}); consistency then follows from the SLLN. For the bias, since ff is linear in bb, write f⁡(w¯M,g¯M)=g¯M⋅h⁡(w¯M)f(\bar{w}_{M},\bar{g}_{M})=\bar{g}_{M}\cdot h(\bar{w}_{M}) where h⁡(a)=a−qh(a)=a^{-q}. Expanding hh around P𝜽P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}} and separating g¯M=μg+(g¯M−μg)\bar{g}_{M}=\mu_{g}+(\bar{g}_{M}-\mu_{g}) yields the O⁡(1/M)O(\nicefrac{{1}}{{M}}) bias from 𝐕𝐚𝐫⁡(wm)\mathbf{Var}(w_{m}) and 𝐂𝐨𝐯⁡(gm,wm)\mathbf{Cov}(g_{m},w_{m}). The remainder is O⁡(M−2)O(M^{-2}): on the high-probability event {w¯M≥P𝜽/2}\{\bar{w}_{M}\geq P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}/2\} (exponential concentration via wm∈[0,1]w_{m}\in[0,1]), the derivatives of the scalar function hh are bounded and Assumption 2 controls the higher-order terms; Assumption 3 gives w¯M−q≤ϵ−q\bar{w}_{M}^{-q}\leq\epsilon^{-q} everywhere, making the complementary event’s contribution O⁡(ϵ−q​e−c​M)O(\epsilon^{-q}\,e^{-cM}). ∎

The O⁡(1/M)O(\nicefrac{{1}}{{M}}) rate is standard for ratio estimators; the JQJ_{Q}-specific feature is the joint dependence on qq and P𝜽P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}. The bias grows with qq (vanishing at q=0q=0) and explodes as P𝜽→0P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}\to 0 with P𝜽−(q+1)P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{-(q+1)} scaling: the same amplification that enables fast cold-start escape (Theorems 5.1 and 5.2) degrades estimator quality. This predicts intermediate qq outperforms both endpoints in practice  — confirmed in Section 7. The expansion is a fixed-P𝜽P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}, large-MM asymptotic; in the cold-start regime where P𝜽P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}} is small and MM is bounded by compute, it identifies the direction of finite-sample degradation rather than providing a uniform bound.

6.1.3 Variance reduction for GARL

The GARL estimator (9) decomposes into a score-function term (for the sampled 𝐳{{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}) and a pathwise term (for the fixed 𝐲∗{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}); only the score-function term admits baselines. Following Kool et al. (2019), we center the score-function coefficient with a leave-one-out control variate using w¯¬m≜1M−1​∑j≠mwj\bar{w}_{\neg m}\triangleq\tfrac{1}{M-1}\sum_{j\neq m}w_{j}, yielding the RLOO estimator (derivation in Section D.1):

∇𝜽ℓq^RLOO=1M∑m=1M[−(wm(w¯M)q−(w¯¬m)1−q)⏟centered weight⋅∇𝜽logp𝜽(𝐳(m)∣𝐱∗)−∇𝜽wm(w¯M)q].\widehat{\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}\ell_{q}}^{\mathrm{RLOO}}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\Bigg[-\underbrace{\biggl(\frac{w_{m}}{(\bar{w}_{M})^{q}}-(\bar{w}_{\neg m})^{1-q}\biggr)}_{\text{centered weight}}\cdot\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}\log p_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}({{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}^{(m)}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*})-\frac{\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}w_{m}}{(\bar{w}_{M})^{q}}\Bigg]. (12)
6.2RLOO bias preservation.

Under the assumptions of Theorem 6.1, 𝔼⁡[∇𝛉ℓq^RLOO]=𝔼⁡[∇𝛉ℓq^plug​-​in]\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}\ell_{q}}^{\mathrm{RLOO}}]=\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}\ell_{q}}^{\mathrm{plug\text{-}in}}], so the RLOO estimator inherits the bias of Equation 11.

Algorithm 1 summarizes the complete estimator. At q=0q=0 it recovers the Rao–Blackwellized RLOO estimator (Zhou et al., 2026); at q=1q=1 the centered weight becomes wm/w¯M−1w_{m}/\bar{w}_{M}-1, a self-normalizing baseline (details in Section D.1).

6.2 PAFT: Posterior-Attenuated Fine-Tuning

GARL estimates the JQJ_{Q} gradient via the RL factorization: sample rationales from the prior p𝜽​(𝐳∣𝐱∗)p_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}({{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*}), then amplify by P𝜽−qP_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{-q}  — sometimes massively, especially on hard instances. The FT factorization (Equation 5) suggests an alternative: instead of sampling from the prior and amplifying, (approximately) sample from the posterior p𝜽​(𝐳∣𝐱∗,𝐲∗)p_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}({{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*})  — where rationales already agree with the answer  — and attenuate by P𝜽1−q∈[0,1]P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{1-q}\in[0,1].

6.2.1 Posterior form of the gradient

Expanding ∇𝜽ℓ1=−∇𝜽​log​P𝜽\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}\ell_{1}=-\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}\log P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}} as a posterior expectation:

∇𝜽ℓq\displaystyle\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}\ell_{q} =−P𝜽1−q⋅𝔼𝐳∼p𝜽​(𝐳∣𝐱∗,𝐲∗)[∇𝜽logp𝜽(𝐳,𝐲∗∣𝐱∗)].\displaystyle=-P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{1-q}\cdot\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{{{{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}\sim p_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}({{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*})}}[\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}\log p_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}({{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*})]. (13)

Each sample gradient is standard SFT (teacher forcing) on a semantically coherent (input, rationale, answer) triple: the rationale is posterior-weighted toward agreement with 𝐲∗{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}.

Approximate posterior sampling.

Equation 13 requires samples from the posterior p𝜽​(𝐳∣𝐱∗,𝐲∗)p_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}({{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}), which is intractable for autoregressive models where 𝐳{{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}} precedes 𝐲{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}. The framework permits many approximate posterior samplers (learned proposals, MCMC, infilling models); here we use importance resampling (Rubin and Rubin, 1988, IR;) because it reuses GARL’s prior sample pool and wmw_{m} weights with minimal additional compute: resample KK trajectories with replacement, with probability proportional to wmw_{m}. IR guarantees exactly KK resampled trajectories regardless of how small the individual wmw_{m} values are.

The PAFT estimator.

Let 𝐳(1),…,𝐳(K){{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}^{(1)},\ldots,{{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}^{(K)} denote the resampled trajectories. The PAFT gradient estimate is

∇^PAFT=−(w¯M)1−q⋅1K∑k=1K∇𝜽logp𝜽(𝐳(k),𝐲∗∣𝐱∗).\displaystyle\hat{\nabla}_{\text{PAFT}}=-(\bar{w}_{M})^{1-q}\cdot\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}\log p_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}({{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}^{(k)},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*}). (14)

At q=1q=1, the instance weight vanishes (P𝜽1−1=1P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{1-1}=1) and PAFT recovers the E-step of EM (Dempster et al., 1977; Phan et al., 2023); see Section D.2 for all endpoint reductions.

6.2.2 Bias and variance

Conditional on the prior pool {(𝐳(m),wm)}m=1M\{({{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}^{(m)},w_{m})\}_{m=1}^{M}, (w¯M)1−q(\bar{w}_{M})^{1-q} is deterministic and the IR average of fm=∇𝜽​log​p𝜽​(𝐳(m),𝐲∗∣𝐱∗)f_{m}=\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}\log p_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}({{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}^{(m)},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*}) has conditional mean ∑m(wm/∑jwj)​fm=−g¯M/w¯M\sum_{m}(\nicefrac{{w_{m}}}{{\sum_{j}w_{j}}})\,f_{m}=-\nicefrac{{\bar{g}_{M}}}{{\bar{w}_{M}}} (using gm=−wm​fmg_{m}=-w_{m}f_{m}). Hence

𝔼[∇^PAFT∣pool]=−(w¯M)1−q⋅(−g¯M/w¯M)=g¯M(w¯M)q=∇^GARL.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\hat{\nabla}_{\mathrm{PAFT}}\mid\mathrm{pool}]=-(\bar{w}_{M})^{1-q}\cdot\bigl(-\nicefrac{{\bar{g}_{M}}}{{\bar{w}_{M}}}\bigr)=\frac{\bar{g}_{M}}{(\bar{w}_{M})^{q}}=\hat{\nabla}_{\mathrm{GARL}}.

Taking outer expectations gives an exact identity 𝔼⁡[∇^PAFT]=𝔼⁡[∇^GARL]\mathbb{E}[\hat{\nabla}_{\mathrm{PAFT}}]=\mathbb{E}[\hat{\nabla}_{\mathrm{GARL}}] at every finite MM, so PAFT has the same O⁡(q/M​P𝜽q+1)O(\nicefrac{{q}}{{MP_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{q+1}}}) bias as GARL (Theorem 6.1) even though the plug-in (w¯M)1−q(\bar{w}_{M})^{1-q} is individually biased (Jensen). The plug-in bias is exactly canceled by the covariance between (w¯M)1−q(\bar{w}_{M})^{1-q} and the IR average: the Rao–Blackwellization identity fixes the total, so components cannot be analyzed in isolation. By the law of total variance, GARL has strictly lower variance than PAFT (Propositions D.3 and D.4).

Yet PAFT can produce better training dynamics. GARL’s lower variance comes from mixing bad rationales into the gradient with small weights; PAFT excludes them before the gradient is formed. The resampling noise is structured  — preserving the semantic coherence of the FT endpoint  — so PAFT is more stable at warm start despite its higher variance (Section 7). Unlike GARL’s reward-times-score structure, the PAFT gradient is a plain posterior expectation of the complete-data score, with no reward coefficient to center; variance reduction comes from the posterior sampling itself, which excludes bad rationales before they reach the gradient.

7 Empirical Validation

We validate the theoretical predictions and empirical effectiveness of GARL and PAFT on subsets of three reasoning datasets  — FinQA (Chen et al., 2021), HotPotQA (Yang et al., 2018), and MuSiQue (Trivedi et al., 2022)  — using post-trained Qwen 3 0.6B (Yang et al., 2025) under both cold-start and warm-start conditions.

7.1 Experimental setup

Warm-start scenario.

Task inputs are natural-language prompts with standard task descriptions and answer-formatting instructions. The un-adapted model can occasionally produce correct answers (Section 7.3), so reward is not sparse.

Cold-start scenario.

We use linearized problem inputs and outputs as (𝐱∗,𝐲∗)({{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}) pairs with no task description and no answer-formatting instructions. The model must discover both how to solve the problem and how to format the answer; initial success probability P𝜽P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}} is very low.

Datasets.

We sample subsets from the official splits of FinQA, HotPotQA, and MuSiQue. FinQA: train n=6145n=6145, validation n=872n=872, test n=1132n=1132. HotPotQA: train n=9067n=9067, validation n=342n=342, test n=343n=343. MuSiQue: train n=9985n=9985, validation n=579n=579, test n=445n=445. Exact-match training rewards are computed against the gold answer string; evaluation uses substring match (Section 7).

Methods and compute budget.

All methods  — GRPO, GARL, and PAFT  — use the same rollout budget of M=32M=32 latent trajectories per prompt during training and 16 samples per prompt at evaluation, so head-to-head comparisons are fair in compute. GARL (Algorithm 1) uses the RLOO variance reduction (Equation 12); PAFT (Algorithm 2) importance-resamples K=MK=M trajectories from the same pool. We evaluate fixed values of q∈{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0}q\in\{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0\}.

Rationale budget.

We enforce a per-rationale token budget by forcing the model to decode the thinking-end token (</think> for our Qwen experiments) once the allocated thinking budget is exhausted (Muennighoff et al., 2025). The budget varies by dataset: FinQA uses 4​k−1284\text{k}-128 tokens, HotPotQA 3​k−1283\text{k}-128, and MuSiQue 2​k−1282\text{k}-128, where the 128128-token offset reserves space for the answer.

Evaluation.

Training uses exact-match rewards (Section 2). Evaluation uses relaxed substring match  — 𝐲^\hat{{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}} is correct if 𝐲∗{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*} appears as a substring of 𝐲^\hat{{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}}  — so rationale tokens around the answer do not penalize the model. We report pass@1 (p@1; single-sample accuracy), pass@kk (p@kk; best-of-kk, rewards coverage), and maj@kk (m@kk; majority vote over kk samples (Wang et al., 2023), rewards diverse correct trajectories). Reported test numbers are taken from the checkpoint with highest validation maj@16.66 6 All numbers in this paper are single-seed; seed variance and bootstrap confidence intervals are left to revision.

7.2 Cold-start results: the escape-time separation

Cold start tests whether commitment speed, controlled by P𝜽−qP_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{-q}, determines escape from a sparse-reward regime (Theorem 5.2).

Cold-start escape requires large qq.

GRPO, Rao–Blackwellized RLOO (q=0q=0), and all q≤0.5q\leq 0.5 fail entirely  — zero accuracy across all metrics. Rao–Blackwellization replaces the binary reward 𝕀⁡(𝐲^=𝐲∗)\mathbb{I}(\hat{{{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}}={{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}) with its conditional expectation wm=p𝜽​(𝐲∗∣𝐱∗,𝐳(m))w_{m}=p_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}({{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}^{(m)}) (Zhou et al., 2026), reducing variance but not helping escape: the underlying gradient remains ∇𝜽ℓ0=−∇𝜽P𝜽\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}\ell_{0}=-\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}} with dynamics p˙=p2​‖s‖2\dot{p}=p^{2}\|s\|^{2} and no amplification (P𝜽−q=1P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{-q}=1 at q=0q=0; Figure 3). These results suggest that in our setting the cold-start bottleneck is primarily gradient amplification rather than gradient variance. The sharp transition at q=0.75q=0.75 matches Theorem 5.1: the lower bound Ω⁡(p0−(1−q))\Omega(p_{0}^{-(1-q)}) grows rapidly as qq decreases, so for a fixed training budget there is a critical qq below which escape fails.

The density-estimation pole escapes but overshoots.

q=1q=1 successfully escapes cold start on all three benchmarks (Table 2), confirming Theorem 5.2. However, q=0.75q=0.75 achieves higher pass@1 and maj@16 on every benchmark. The pass@16 picture is more nuanced: q=1q=1 achieves higher pass@16 than q=0.75q=0.75 on HotPotQA (75.5 vs. 74.1), consistent with its stronger mode-covering behavior producing more diverse reasoning paths. But this diversity does not translate to higher maj@16, because the trajectories are trained with noisier gradients. This is exactly the escape-vs-bias tradeoff predicted by Theorem 6.1: q=1q=1’s stronger amplification enables faster escape but produces noisier gradient estimates, while q=0.75q=0.75 strikes a better balance.

Cold-start GARL is competitive with prompted GRPO.

Table 2 compares cold-start GARL at q∈{0.75,1}q\in\{0.75,1\} (no task-specific prompts) against warm-start GRPO (with prompts) across all three benchmarks; all methods use exact-match training rewards. In our setting, GARL at q=0.75q=0.75 matches or exceeds prompted GRPO on every metric across all three benchmarks (+11.6+11.6 p@1 on FinQA, +24.4+24.4 on HotPotQA, +13.2+13.2 on MuSiQue), and GARL at q=1q=1 exceeds GRPO on coverage metrics (p@16, m@16) while underperforming on p@1. We treat this as a hypothesis-generating observation rather than evidence that prompts are unnecessary: cold- and warm-start runs differ in more than prompts (input formatting, output constraints, target distribution), and isolating the prompt factor requires a controlled ablation we leave to future work.

7.3 Warm-start results across three benchmarks

Warm start tests whether GARL and PAFT still help when P𝜽P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}} is not negligible and standard RL already makes progress. Table 3 reports warm-start maj@16 across all three benchmarks.

Cold-start without instructions beats warm-start with them.

The base model with task-specific prompts but no training performs weakly (12.6 / 22.2 / 8.9 maj@16; first row of Table 3), confirming that these tasks require adaptation. Every trained method in Tables 2 and 3 improves over this base. More striking: cold-start GARL at q=0.75q=0.75 without any task-specific prompts matches or beats the best stable warm-start maj@16 on every benchmark  — FinQA 38.3 vs. 38.7 (tie with warm-start GARL at q=0.25q=0.25), HotPotQA 57.2 vs. 47.9 (+9.3+9.3), MuSiQue 34.8 vs. 22.4 (+12.4+12.4).

The swing from base-with-prompts to cold-start GARL is +25.7+25.7 to +35.0+35.0 points with no prompt engineering whatsoever. Instructions and answer-formatting supervision are not merely unnecessary under strong commitment; one interpretation is that the added prompt structure may constrain the learned policy toward narrower reasoning patterns. A controlled ablation isolating the prompt factor from other cold-start/warm-start differences is left to future work. With high-qq amplification, the model discovers task structure directly from input-output pairs.

Rao–Blackwellized rewards alone are insufficient.

GARL at q=0q=0 recovers the Rao–Blackwellized REINFORCE estimator of Zhou et al. (2026) with leave-one-out baseline (RB-RLOO). It beats GRPO on FinQA (+11.4+11.4 m@16) but underperforms on HotPotQA (−11.9-11.9) and MuSiQue (−6.7-6.7): replacing the binary reward with wm=p𝜽​(𝐲∗∣𝐱∗,𝐳)w_{m}=p_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}({{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}) does not generalize across warm-start tasks. Raising qq lifts peak accuracy on the unstable benchmarks (GARL q=0.75q=0.75: HotPotQA 21.6→46.821.6\to 46.8 peak; MuSiQue 9.1→19.79.1\to 19.7 peak; FinQA is roughly flat across q∈[0,0.75]q\in[0,0.75]), but peaks do not survive training on HotPotQA or MuSiQue (next paragraphs).

Low qq wins on FinQA.

On FinQA, GARL is stable throughout training at all tested qq, so the cost of high qq  — estimator bias O⁡(q/M​P𝜽q+1)O(\nicefrac{{q}}{{MP_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{q+1}}}) (Theorem 6.1) and noise memorization (Proposition C.2), both driven by P𝜽−qP_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{-q}  — outweighs its amplification benefit, and lower-bias estimators extract more signal per step. GARL at q=0.25q=0.25 posts the best FinQA maj@16 (38.7, +11.8+11.8 over GRPO). On MuSiQue and HotPotQA, GARL’s warm-start training collapses (next paragraphs), so this low-qq advantage cannot be realized without training-dynamics instability.

GARL destabilizes on HotPotQA; PAFT is stable.

GARL destabilizes on HotPotQA warm-start at every tested qq: validation accuracy peaks early and collapses to zero before the end of training (q=0.2q=0.2: peak 41.1 at step 100, zero by step 150; q=0.25q=0.25: peak 22.9 at step 50, zero by step 100; q=0.75q=0.75: peak 46.8 at step 50, zero by step 100). HotPotQA exhibits broader instability  — GRPO also degrades, peaking at ∼\sim37.4 around step 100 and declining steadily to ∼\sim5.0 by end of training  — but GARL’s collapse is qualitatively different: a sharp drop to literal zero rather than a gradual decline. PAFT shows neither pattern, reaching 47.9 maj@16 (+14.4+14.4 over GRPO) and remaining stable. Figure 4 compares GARL and PAFT validation curves at matched q=0.25q=0.25. We do not have a verified mechanism for the GARL-specific zero-collapse: candidate explanations include pathwise-term corruption (the GARL gradient updates p𝜽​(𝐲∗∣𝐱∗,𝐳)p_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}({{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}) on every sampled 𝐳{{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}, including incoherent ones, while PAFT only updates on resampled coherent rationales) and HotPotQA-specific overfitting (also visible in GRPO), and disentangling them would require a pathwise-zeroed ablation and additional diagnostics. The practical implication holds regardless: PAFT is the stable choice on benchmarks where GARL collapses.

PAFT at low qq is slow, not collapsed.

PAFT at q=0.25q=0.25 underperforms on MuSiQue (9.0 vs. 15.8), but validation accuracy is still rising at the end of training rather than dropping: the attenuation factor P𝜽1−q=P𝜽0.75P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{1-q}=P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{0.75} heavily down-weights hard instances, so learning is slow but not unstable. This differs qualitatively from GARL’s warm-start collapse on HotPotQA and MuSiQue (validation drops to zero). The GARL-vs-PAFT trade-off is therefore speed vs. stability: PAFT gives up gradient signal per step but avoids the destabilization observed in GARL on HotPotQA and MuSiQue. Raising qq to 0.75 recovers speed for PAFT without compromising stability, delivering best-overall HotPotQA (47.9) and the honest MuSiQue recommendation (22.4 steady-state vs. GARL’s 24.3 peak-before-collapse).

7.4 Discussion

GARL and PAFT trade speed against stability. Across regimes: cold start requires GARL’s amplification (PAFT is undefined when P𝜽≈0P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}\approx 0); warm start admits both. Within warm start: GARL delivers higher per-step signal but destabilizes during training on HotPotQA and MuSiQue (collapse to zero), where HotPotQA also exhibits broader instability visible in GRPO’s gradual decline. PAFT does not collapse on any benchmark tested, at the cost of lower per-step signal (P𝜽1−qP_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{1-q} attenuation plus posterior-resampling variance). On these benchmarks, the practical decision is stable-vs-not rather than high-qq-vs-low-qq: use GARL at low qq where it is stable (FinQA); use PAFT at q≥0.75q\geq 0.75 where GARL collapses (HotPotQA, MuSiQue). The mechanism behind GARL’s zero-collapse is unverified; pathwise-term corruption and dataset-specific overfitting are both candidates that future ablations could disentangle.

Practical recommendation: GARL at large qq for cold-start escape; in warm start, use GARL at low qq if training is stable (FinQA), and PAFT at q≥0.75q\geq 0.75 otherwise (HotPotQA, MuSiQue). PAFT also acts as an automatic curriculum: early on, only the easiest rationales pass the importance resampling filter; as P𝜽P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}} grows, more rationales become coherent enough to be selected, broadening the training distribution without an explicit schedule.

8 Related Work

qq-logarithmic losses.

The Tsallis qq-logarithm originates in non-extensive statistical mechanics (Tsallis, 1988). Ferrari and Yang (2010) introduced the maximum LqL_{q}-likelihood estimator (MLqE), which replaces log\log with logq\log_{q} in the log-likelihood and is equivalent to reweighting the score by f​(X,θ)1−qf(X;\theta)^{1-q}. For sample-size-dependent qn→1q_{n}\to 1, MLqE is asymptotically normal around θ0\theta_{0}; for fixed q<1q<1, finite-sample MSE can fall below MLE’s at the cost of bias toward a surrogate parameter θ0/q\theta_{0}/q. The PAFT gradient Equation 13 is the marginal-likelihood analog of this weighted score. Extending the qq-log to deep classification, Zhang and Sabuncu (2018) proposed generalized cross-entropy for noisy labels (the same loss family under a different parameterization), observing that bounded loss at q<1q<1 prevents gradient domination by mislabeled samples. Our escort minimizer analysis (Theorem 3.1) gives a precise mechanism: the tempering α~j1/q\tilde{\alpha}_{j}^{\nicefrac{{1}}{{q}}} concentrates the minimizer on the clean mode. Concurrently, Wang et al. (2026) apply the deformed-log family at the token level for SFT, deriving a gate-times-error gradient structure; their token-level gate pαp^{\alpha} is the single-token specialization of our example-level P𝜽−qP_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{-q}, but their pp is an exact softmax probability whereas our P𝜽P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}} is an intractable marginal over latent trajectories.

Training-time exploration-exploitation.

Tsallis entropy has been used as a policy regularizer in RL (Lee et al., 2018; Nachum et al., 2018), providing inference-time exploration through sparse action distributions. Our use of the Tsallis qq-logarithm in the loss function provides a different kind of control: training-time exploration-exploitation. The escort minimizer θj∗∝αj1/q\theta_{j}^{*}\propto\alpha_{j}^{1/q} (Theorem 3.1) is a training-time analog of inference temperature that permanently shapes what the model learns, and the P𝜽−qP_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{-q} factor automatically explores more on instances the model finds surprising  — a per-instance effect not achievable by tuning the learning rate or inference temperature alone.

Information-theoretic context.

Escort distributions were studied by Beck and Schögl (1993). Rényi variational inference (Li and Turner, 2016) provides a complementary continuum that tightens the ELBO toward exact log-marginal-likelihood; our JQJ_{Q} family approaches the same target from the exploitation side, with −log⁡P𝜽-\log P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}} as their shared meeting point. The RL-as-inference connection (Levine, 2018; Norouzi et al., 2016; Guu et al., 2017) views MLE and RL as distinct frameworks; our contribution is embedding them as endpoints of a single continuously parameterized family.

Latent-variable training for reasoning.

On the RL side, RLVR and GRPO (DeepSeek-AI, 2025; Shao et al., 2024) optimize expected reward with policy gradients. On the latent-variable side, STaR (Zelikman et al., 2022) bootstraps reasoning by generating and filtering rationales, while TRICE (Phan et al., 2023) maximizes marginal log-likelihood via MCMC-EM. Our framework subsumes these as endpoints: RLVR corresponds to q=0q=0 and marginal log-likelihood training to q=1q=1. PAFT at q=1q=1 recovers the EM E-step underlying TRICE, and STaR’s rejection-sampling strategy can be viewed as a hard-acceptance variant of PAFT’s importance resampling (Section D.2).

Concurrent RL-to-ML interpolations.

MaxRL (Tajwar et al., 2026) defines another RL-to-ML continuum by truncating the Maclaurin expansion of log⁡p\log p at order TT. Their estimator is unbiased for the truncated objective J(T)J^{(T)} (itself a biased approximation of log⁡P𝜽\log P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}), while GARL targets the true qq-loss with O⁡(1/M)O(\nicefrac{{1}}{{M}}) estimator bias (Theorem 6.1). A key distinction is cold-start behavior: the MaxRL estimator is exactly zero when no sample succeeds (K=0K{=}0), while GARL always has nonzero gradient since wm>0w_{m}>0. MaxRL and PAFT share the principle of training on successful trajectories; in the limit T→∞T\to\infty and q=1q=1, both average posterior-sampled gradients, differing only in hard (MaxRL) vs. soft (PAFT) acceptance.

Gradient estimators for marginal likelihoods.

The IWAE estimator (Burda et al., 2015) that GARL recovers at q=1q{=}1 has a well-known failure mode: Rainforth et al. (2018) showed that as MM grows, the signal-to-noise ratio of the inference-network gradient shrinks, motivating doubly reparameterized variants (Roeder et al., 2017; Tucker et al., 2019). Our bias expansion O⁡(q/M​P𝜽q+1)O(\nicefrac{{q}}{{MP_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{q+1}}}) exposes a related phenomenon along the JQJ_{Q} continuum: the same amplification that enables cold-start escape degrades estimator quality, and intermediate qq balances the two  — a prediction confirmed in Section 7.

Rao–Blackwellization and verifier-free training.

Zhou et al. (2026) propose VeriFree, which uses p𝜽​(𝐲∗∣𝐱∗,𝐳)p_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}({{\bm{\mathbf{y}}}}^{*}\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*},{{\bm{\mathbf{z}}}}) directly as the reward signal. This is the RB-REINFORCE estimator that GARL recovers at q=0q=0 (Section 6.1). While Rao–Blackwellization reduces gradient variance, our experimental results in Section 7 show it does not address the cold-start escape bottleneck: the gradient remains ∇𝜽ℓ0=−∇𝜽P𝜽\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}\ell_{0}=-\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}} regardless of Rao–Blackwellization, and the dynamics p˙=p2​‖s‖2\dot{p}=p^{2}\|s\|^{2} receive no amplification at q=0q=0 (Figure 3). Both GARL and PAFT are verifier-free throughout the JQJ_{Q} continuum.

RLVR capability boundaries and reward hacking.

Yue et al. (2025) showed that RLVR improves sampling efficiency but rarely elicits new reasoning patterns, and the capability boundary narrows during training. Our framework gives a direct mechanism: this narrowing is the mode-seeking behavior predicted by the escort distribution at q=0q=0 (Corollary B.2). Related, sustained GRPO training with exact-match rewards often collapses via reward hacking, where models exploit verifier formatting rather than reasoning. The JQJ_{Q} continuum exposes qq as a principled control for mode concentration, and PAFT as an empirically more stable alternative to GARL during warm-start training (Section 7).

9 Conclusion and Future Work

We introduced a Tsallis loss continuum JQJ_{Q} that unifies RLVR-style exploitation and marginal-likelihood training via a single parameter qq controlling commitment to unfamiliar supervision. The per-instance amplification P𝜽−qP_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{-q} is the mechanism that addresses the cold-start stalling problem: GARL at large qq escapes cold start where GRPO fails, and the Ω⁡(1/p0)\Omega(\nicefrac{{1}}{{p_{0}}}) lower bound for RLVR-style training is bypassed by moving qq away from the exploitation pole. The gradient admits a dual factorization through the RL and FT endpoints (Proposition 4.1), yielding two complementary estimators: GARL (prior-sampling amplification) and PAFT (posterior-sampling attenuation). High commitment (q→1q\to 1) resolves ambiguity but memorizes noise; low commitment (q→0q\to 0) resolves noise but cannot escape cold start. Within warm start, GARL destabilizes on HotPotQA and MuSiQue while PAFT remains stable across all benchmarks tested.

Limitations and future work.

Experiments in this work use a single model scale (Qwen 3 0.6B), three benchmarks, and fixed values of qq. The cold-start escape theorems and bias expansion are scale-agnostic, but the GARL collapse / PAFT stability finding has been verified only at this scale; replication at bigger model scales is important. Our convergence analysis is stylized: single-example, gradient flow, bounded score (Theorems 5.1 and 5.2). Our framework assumes exact-match supervision (Section 2); extension to general rewards is open.

Appendix C Proofs for Section 5: Commitment Dynamics under Gradient Flow

C.1 Warm-up: exact analysis on the sigmoid model

Before proving the general results, we work through the scalar sigmoid model P⁡(θ)=σ⁡(θ)=(1+e−θ)−1P(\theta)=\sigma(\theta)=(1+e^{-\theta})^{-1} as a warm-up. This model admits exact closed-form escape times that validate the Θ⁡(⋅)\Theta(\cdot) bounds in Theorem 5.2.

Under gradient flow on ℓq​(θ)=−logq⁡(σ⁡(θ))\ell_{q}(\theta)=-\log_{q}(\sigma(\theta)), the parameter evolves as θ˙=P​(θ)−q​P′​(θ)\dot{\theta}=P(\theta)^{-q}P^{\prime}(\theta). Since P′​(θ)=P⁡(θ)​(1−P⁡(θ))P^{\prime}(\theta)=P(\theta)(1-P(\theta)), the chain rule gives:

p˙=[P′​(θ)]2​P​(θ)−q=p2−q​(1−p)2.\displaystyle\dot{p}=[P^{\prime}(\theta)]^{2}P(\theta)^{-q}=p^{2-q}(1-p)^{2}.

C.5 Noise-fitting rate under symmetric label noise

The cold-start escape rates (Theorems 5.1 and 5.2) measure how fast the model commits to correct supervision under the JQJ_{Q} amplification P𝜽−qP_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}^{-q}. The symmetric question is how fast the model commits to incorrect supervision: the same amplification drives both, giving the following dynamical formulation of robustness under label noise.

Noise-contamination setup.

We work with a two-label categorical model, chosen to expose the mechanism in the simplest possible setting. For a single input 𝐱∗{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*}, the model predicts one of two labels {c,k}\{c,k\} with probabilities p𝜽​(c∣𝐱∗)=pp_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}(c\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*})=p and p𝜽​(k∣𝐱∗)=1−pp_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}(k\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*})=1-p, where pp is a differentiable function of 𝜽∈ℝd{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. The target label is corrupted: with probability 1−ϵ1-\epsilon it equals the clean value cc, and with probability ϵ∈(0,1/2)\epsilon\in(0,1/2) it flips to the noise value kk, giving α~=(1−ϵ,ϵ)\tilde{\alpha}=(1-\epsilon,\epsilon). The restriction to two labels is cosmetic: in the NN-label categorical model with symmetric noise α~=(1−ϵ)​α+ϵ⋅Unif\tilde{\alpha}=(1-\epsilon)\alpha+\epsilon\cdot\mathrm{Unif}, conditioning on the two-subset {j∗,k}\{j^{*},k\} containing the clean mode j∗j^{*} and any fixed wrong label kk reduces to this binary setting.

Let p⁡(t)=p𝜽​(c∣𝐱∗)p(t)=p_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}(c\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*}) denote the clean-mode probability under gradient flow on JQ​(𝜽)=𝔼y∼α~​[ℓq​(p𝜽​(y∣𝐱∗))]J_{Q}({\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}})=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\tilde{\alpha}}[\ell_{q}(p_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}(y\mid{{\bm{\mathbf{x}}}}^{*}))], and let p~​(t)=1−p​(t)\tilde{p}(t)=1-p(t) denote the noise contamination. As in Appendix C, we assume bounded score: c∗≤‖s⁡(𝜽⁡(t))‖≤Cc_{*}\leq\|s({\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}(t))\|\leq C where s≜∇𝜽​log​ps\triangleq\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}\log p is the score of the clean-mode probability (the analog of ∇𝜽​log​P𝜽\nabla_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}\log P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}} in Section 5).

The escort asymptote.

Differentiating J⁡(p)=(1−ϵ)​ℓq​(p)+ϵ​ℓq​(1−p)J(p)=(1-\epsilon)\ell_{q}(p)+\epsilon\ell_{q}(1-p) gives J′​(p)=−(1−ϵ)​p−q+ϵ​p~−qJ^{\prime}(p)=-(1-\epsilon)p^{-q}+\epsilon\tilde{p}^{-q}. Gradient flow on a scalar parameterization of pp yields

p~˙=−p˙=[ϵ​p~−q−(1−ϵ)​(1−p~)−q]​p2​‖s‖2.\displaystyle\dot{\tilde{p}}=-\dot{p}=[\epsilon\tilde{p}^{-q}-(1-\epsilon)(1-\tilde{p})^{-q}]\,p^{2}\,\|s\|^{2}. (16)

For q>0q>0, the dynamics have a unique stable equilibrium at

p~∗​(q)≜(ϵ/(1−ϵ))1/q​(1+o⁡(1))as ​ϵ→0,\displaystyle\tilde{p}_{*}(q)\;\triangleq\;(\epsilon/(1-\epsilon))^{1/q}\,(1+o(1))\quad\text{as }\epsilon\to 0, (17)

obtained by solving J′​(p)=0J^{\prime}(p)=0. This equilibrium coincides with the static escort minimizer from Theorem 3.1 applied to α~\tilde{\alpha}: at q=1q=1, p~∗​(1)=ϵ\tilde{p}_{*}(1)=\epsilon (the model fits observed noise exactly); as q→0q\to 0, p~∗​(q)→0\tilde{p}_{*}(q)\to 0 (the model concentrates on the clean mode, paralleling Corollary B.2). The escort is both where JQJ_{Q} is minimized (static) and where gradient flow converges (dynamic).

The noise-to-clean ratio ϵ​p~−q/[(1−ϵ)​(1−p~)−q]\epsilon\tilde{p}^{-q}/[(1-\epsilon)(1-\tilde{p})^{-q}] is monotone decreasing in p~\tilde{p} on (0,1)(0,1): it diverges as p~→0\tilde{p}\to 0 (noise term dominates near the clean mode), equals 11 at p~=p~∗​(q)\tilde{p}=\tilde{p}_{*}(q) (equilibrium), and vanishes as p~→1\tilde{p}\to 1. So for p~≪p~∗​(q)\tilde{p}\ll\tilde{p}_{*}(q)  — the regime of small noise contamination  — the noise term in Equation 16 dominates by an arbitrarily large factor. This drives the asymptotic scaling.

C.2Noise-fitting rate.

Fix q∈(0,1]q\in(0,1]. Under the setup above, starting from p~​(0)=0+\tilde{p}(0)=0^{+}, the time Tqnoise​(η)T_{q}^{\mathrm{noise}}(\eta) to reach noise contamination level p~​(Tqnoise)=η\tilde{p}(T_{q}^{\mathrm{noise}})=\eta satisfies, for η\eta below the stable equilibrium (i.e. η≪p~∗​(q)\eta\ll\tilde{p}_{*}(q); in particular as η→0\eta\to 0):

p~˙∈[(1−1K)​ϵ​c∗2​p~−q​(1+o⁡(1)),ϵ​C2​p~−q].\displaystyle\dot{\tilde{p}}\;\in\;\bigl[(1-\tfrac{1}{K})\,\epsilon\,c_{*}^{2}\,\tilde{p}^{-q}\,(1+o(1)),\;\epsilon\,C^{2}\,\tilde{p}^{-q}\bigr].

Fix any K>1K>1 (e.g., K=2K=2). Theorem 5.2 gives Tqescape​(p0)=Θ⁡(p0−(1−q)/(1−q))T_{q}^{\mathrm{escape}}(p_{0})=\Theta(p_{0}^{-(1-q)}/(1-q)) for q<1q<1 with speedup ratio Tq/Tq′=Θ⁡(p0−(q′−q))T_{q}/T_{q^{\prime}}=\Theta(p_{0}^{-(q^{\prime}-q)}). The factor (g¯M−μg)=Op(M−1/2)(\bar{g}_{M}-\mu_{g})=O_{p}(M^{-1/2}), so a second-order expansion of h⁡(w¯M)h(\bar{w}_{M}) suffices. Multiplying (g¯M−μg)(\bar{g}_{M}-\mu_{g}) by each term of the expansion and taking expectations:

𝔼[(g¯M−μg)​h​(w¯M)]\displaystyle\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[(\bar{g}_{M}-\mu_{g})\,h(\bar{w}_{M})]
=h⁡(μw)​𝔼[g¯M−μg]⏟=0+h′​(μw)​𝔼[(g¯M−μg)​(w¯M−μw)]⏟=−qM​μw−q−1​𝐂𝐨𝐯​(gm,wm)\displaystyle=\underbrace{h(\mu_{w})\,\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[\bar{g}_{M}-\mu_{g}]}_{=0}+\underbrace{h^{\prime}(\mu_{w})\,\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[(\bar{g}_{M}-\mu_{g})(\bar{w}_{M}-\mu_{w})]}_{=-\frac{q}{M}\mu_{w}^{-q-1}\mathbf{Cov}(g_{m},w_{m})}

For the cross moment, expand 𝔼[(g¯M−μg)​(w¯M−μw)2]=M−3​∑i,j,k𝔼[(gi−μg)​(wj−μw)​(wk−μw)]\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[(\bar{g}_{M}-\mu_{g})(\bar{w}_{M}-\mu_{w})^{2}]=M^{-3}\sum_{i,j,k}\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[(g_{i}-\mu_{g})(w_{j}-\mu_{w})(w_{k}-\mu_{w})]. By independence, the only nonzero index pattern is i=j=ki=j=k (all others vanish because 𝔼[gi−μg]=0\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[g_{i}-\mu_{g}]=0 or 𝔼[wj−μw]=0\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[w_{j}-\mu_{w}]=0). The MM surviving terms give 𝔼[(gm−μg)​(wm−μw)2]/M2=O⁡(M−2)\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[(g_{m}-\mu_{g})(w_{m}-\mu_{w})^{2}]/M^{2}=O(M^{-2}), since |(wm−μw)2|≤1|(w_{m}-\mu_{w})^{2}|\leq 1 and 𝔼[‖gm‖]<∞\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[\|g_{m}\|]<\infty (Assumption 2). Combining.

Adding the two pieces and substituting μw=P𝜽\mu_{w}=P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}, μg=∇𝜽ℓ0\mu_{g}=\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}\ell_{0}, ∇𝜽ℓ1=∇𝜽ℓ0/P𝜽\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}\ell_{1}=\nicefrac{{\nabla_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}\ell_{0}}}{{P_{{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}}}}:

Remainder bound.

Write 𝔼[RM]=𝔼[RM⋅𝟏A]+𝔼[RM⋅𝟏Ac]\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[R_{M}]=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[R_{M}\cdot\mathbf{1}_{A}]+\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[R_{M}\cdot\mathbf{1}_{A^{c}}] where A={w¯M≥P𝜽/2}A=\{\bar{w}_{M}\geq P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}/2\}.

On AA. The derivatives of hh are bounded on {a≥P𝜽/2}\{a\geq P_{\bm{\mathbf{\theta}}}/2\}: |h(k)​(a)|≤Ck|h^{(k)}(a)|\leq C_{k}.

For RM(1)R_{M}^{(1)} (the fourth-order scalar remainder), the integral form gives |RM(1)|≤C4​|w¯M−μw|4|R_{M}^{(1)}|\leq C_{4}|\bar{w}_{M}-\mu_{w}|^{4} on AA. Since wm∈[0,1]w_{m}\in[0{,}1], 𝔼[|w¯M−μw|4]=O⁡(M−2)\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[|\bar{w}_{M}-\mu_{w}|^{4}]=O(M^{-2}), so 𝔼[|RM(1)|⋅𝟏A]=O⁡(M−2)\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[|R_{M}^{(1)}|\cdot\mathbf{1}_{A}]=O(M^{-2}).

For RM(2)=(g¯M−μg)⋅O⁡(|w¯M−μw|3)R_{M}^{(2)}=(\bar{g}_{M}-\mu_{g})\cdot O(|\bar{w}_{M}-\mu_{w}|^{3}) on AA (the third-order remainder from the second piece), Cauchy–Schwarz gives 𝔼[|RM(2)|⋅𝟏A]≤C3𝔼[‖g¯M−μg‖2]𝔼[(w¯M−μw)6]=O(M−1/2)O(M−3/2)=O(M−2)\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[|R_{M}^{(2)}|\cdot\mathbf{1}_{A}]\leq C_{3}\,\sqrt{\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[\|\bar{g}_{M}-\mu_{g}\|^{2}]}\,\sqrt{\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[(\bar{w}_{M}-\mu_{w})^{6}]}=O(M^{-1/2})\,O(M^{-3/2})=O(M^{-2}), using Assumption 2 and the boundedness of wmw_{m}.

Therefore |RM|≤|f⁡(w¯M,g¯M)|+|TM|≤C​ϵ−q​(1+‖g¯M‖)|R_{M}|\leq|f(\bar{w}_{M},\bar{g}_{M})|+|T_{M}|\leq C\,\epsilon^{-q}\,(1+\|\bar{g}_{M}\|), where TMT_{M} collects the (bounded) Taylor terms. 𝔼[|RM|⋅𝟏Ac]\displaystyle\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[|R_{M}|\cdot\mathbf{1}_{A^{c}}] ≤C​ϵ−q​𝔼[(1+‖g¯M‖)2]​P⁡(Ac).\displaystyle\leq C\,\epsilon^{-q}\,\sqrt{\mathop{\mathbb{E}}[(1+\|\bar{g}_{M}\|)^{2}]}\,\sqrt{P(A^{c})}.

The first factor is O⁡(1)O(1) by Assumption 2.
